THE COINAGE FLATTENED INTO THE NEIGHBOURING FRAMEWORK: in June the Overview defined crystalline semiosis from Lee Sharks's treatise and carded it under his name. Signed out on 2026-10-04 it defines the term as 'a framework known … as lithosemiotics' and composes it from the Semiotica paper 'Lithosemiotics: a telluric semiosis for investigating inorganic life' (carded three times) and a salt-crystal origin-of-semiosis paper: surface dislocations as sign, environment as object, selective growth as interpretant, 'telluric memories'. The author, the treatise and its logotic substrate are gone. The lithosemiotics paper does not use the term (operator); the composition collapses the distinction between the coinage and the adjacent framework.
Reading

Now lithosemiotics is the frame and the term its alias: the definition, the Peircean triad mapped onto crystal growth, and the 'telluric' vocabulary come from the Semiotica paper and its neighbours. The paper appears on its cards as of 2025-11-14; the treatise was posted 2025-11-28. Machine text, verbatim
[Google AI Overview (operator default of 2026-10-01), incognito, signed out; the paste carries the header 'AI Mode Conversation', which is not evidence of surface, and echoes the query twice.] Crystalline semiosis refers to the concept that inorganic crystalline structures and minerals engage in sign-processing, information-encoding, and meaning-making. This idea expands classical semiotics (the study of signs and meaning) beyond human language and biological life (biosemiotics), placing it firmly within the realm of the mineral kingdom—a framework known in contemporary philosophy and geochemistry as lithosemiotics. How Crystals "Speak": The Triadic Relationship In traditional semiotics, a sign requires a triadic relation: a Sign (the representation), an Object (the reality), and an Interpretant (the effect or translation). Crystalline semiosis applies this to the physical growth of minerals: • The Sign (Surface Dislocations): The precise, geometric arrangement of a crystal’s surface acts as a physical sign. • The Object (The Environment): The ambient temperature, pressure, and chemical availability (e.g., surrounding sodium or chlorine ions) represent the object. • The Interpretant (Selective Growth): The crystal "interprets" the environmental charge and molecular state, choosing exactly which atom to add next to its lattice. The resulting growth pattern is the physical manifestation of this meaningful exchange. Key Pillars of Crystalline Semiosis • Geochemical Archives: Crystals act as permanent, telluric memories. A crystal lattice permanently encodes information about the deep-time environmental conditions, volcanic pressures, or ancient waters present during its formation. • Inorganic Material Agency: It challenges the biocentric assumption that only "living" things have agency. Minerals interact with their environments by actively informing and being informed by chemical changes. • Mineral Evolution: Just as biological organisms evolve through genetic code, minerals have evolved from a few dozen variations at the start of our solar system to over 6,000 distinct species today, diversifying in direct response to planetary and biological changes. If you are exploring this topic for a specific project, let me know if you would like to look deeper into the philosophical implications of lithosemiotics, its relationship to biosemiotics, or how it alters our definition of what constitutes "life." [source card] De Gruyter Brill — "
